Form the past Konjunktiv II with modals: hätte + infinitive + infinitive of the modal (double infinitive).
Express reproaches: Du hättest anrufen sollen!
Express regrets: Ich hätte mehr lernen müssen.
Talk about missed opportunities: Wir hätten fliegen können.
Put “hätte” in the right place in a subordinate clause: …, dass er hätte anrufen sollen.
It's April 2033. Thomas's family is moving to Berlin, into a house in Treptow. The removal van has just left. Leo, 17, tells his father what he wants to do after school. Ludwig is listening.
Dad, I have to tell you something. I've applied to the BVG. For an apprenticeship as a tram driver. Starting in September.
What? Without talking to me? Leo, you should have asked me first!
I knew what you'd say. You'd have said: better study mechanical engineering. Like you.
Of course! With your grades you could study anything. You could have applied to any university!
But I don't want to study. I want to drive trams. Like Grandpa.
May I say something? Thomas, do you still remember what we argued about in 1997?
I haven't. You wanted to study in Munich. And I wanted you to stay and start at the BVG. I said: there are enough engineers. I shouldn't have said that.
I should have supported you. Instead we hardly spoke for thirty years. Don't make the same mistake, just the other way round.
You're right. Leo, I… I shouldn't have raised my voice. Tell me about this apprenticeship. How long does it take?
Three years. And Grandpa, Mr Wolff said that if I pass the exam, I'm allowed to drive the Tatra 5218 once.
“hätte … nicht … dürfen” = shouldn't have (wasn't allowed to)
“hätte … müssen” = should have, would have had to
“HET-uh … ZOL-en”: stress on “hätte” and on the main verb.
In the past Konjunktiv II with a modal verb, you DON'T use the participle of the modal, but its infinitive. This gives a “double infinitive” at the end:
Du hättest fragen sollen. (you should have)
Das hätte ich nicht sagen dürfen.
Not “Du hättest fragen gesollt” ✗. With another verb, the modal stays in the infinitive: “…fragen sollen” ✓.
Wir hätten fliegen können, aber wir sind gefahren.
something forbidden that was done anyway
“hätte … können” can also express something that almost happened: “Das hätte gefährlich werden können!” = That could have been dangerous!
Word-order exception: with a double infinitive, “hätte” does NOT go to the end, but in front of the two infinitives:
I know I should have supported you.
He says he should have called earlier.
The same rule applies to the Perfekt with modals: “…, weil er nicht hat kommen können.” The conjugated verb jumps in front of the group of infinitives.
To soften a reproach: “Vielleicht hättest du … sollen.” / “Es wäre besser gewesen, wenn …”
You should have come on time!
I know I should have studied more.
I should have told you that.
We could have taken the train.

The Brandts' new house was in Treptow, not far from the Spree, an old terraced house with a small garden and an apple tree that was just beginning to blossom. The removal van from Munich had arrived at eight in the morning, and by midday four men, Thomas, Paul, Andrei and Jakob, had carried a hundred and seventy crates, two sofas, a piano and a washing machine into the house. Leo had helped too, but he had been quiet all morning. Too quiet, Anja thought. She knew her son. When he was that quiet, he was carrying something around with him.

Ludwig had come with Elif and Lena, by tram, of course, and with a basket full of rolls from the café. He was now sitting on an upturned moving box in the garden, under the apple tree, watching the others work. He had seen Thomas almost every week since Christmas. Since Thomas had been working in Adlershof, he came to Kastanienallee every Friday after work, had a coffee at the café, ate a slice of apple cake and talked about his week. Ludwig had waited thirty-six years for these Fridays.

Elif was running round the garden examining every bush, every flower, every stone. She had found out from Lena that Leo wanted to start at the BVG in September, maybe, and that this was a secret, and she was almost bursting with importance. Twice she had nearly let it slip. Once, when Thomas asked if anyone was thirsty, she said: “Leo's definitely thirsty, because soon he has to…”, and then put her own hand over her mouth and ran off into the garden. Lena laughed so hard she had to sit down.

The row came in the afternoon, when the last crates were in the house and everyone was sitting in the garden. Leo couldn't hold out any longer. He had simply said it, in the middle of a conversation about his new school, which he would go to from May for the last few months before his Abitur. And Thomas, who had been in a good mood all day, first went pale, then red, then raised his voice. Louder than Anja had ever heard him in twenty-five years of marriage. The neighbours in the next garden stopped talking.

“An apprenticeship?” shouted Thomas. “You've got a 1.3 average on your report! You could study medicine! Do you know how many young people would love that? You could at least have waited until we could talk about it calmly!” Leo looked at the ground. “We've never talked calmly about anything, Dad,” he said quietly. “You always knew what was right before I'd said anything.” Anja put her hand on her husband's arm, but he shook it off, not nastily, just impatiently, as he always did when he knew someone was right and didn't want to admit it.

And then Ludwig said, calmly, from his moving box, the sentence about 1997. And everyone fell silent. Paul and Andrei looked at each other. Lena took Elif by the hand and went into the kitchen with her to make coffee, even though nobody wanted coffee. Anja sat down next to her husband. And Thomas looked at his father as if he had never seen him before.

Even Elif, who otherwise could never sit still, stayed in the kitchen doorway holding the coffee pot with both hands, as if she were afraid of dropping it. In the apple tree a blackbird was singing, as if nothing had happened.

Ludwig went on, slowly, as if he had to take each word separately out of an old crate. How in 1997 he had sat at the kitchen table every evening imagining his son in the driver's cab, on the same line, at the same stops, and how proud he would have been. How Thomas had come home one evening with the letter from the University of Munich, beaming, and how Ludwig, instead of congratulating him, had said: “There are enough engineers. Not enough good tram drivers.” And how Thomas had put the letter on the table and gone to his room without a word. “That was the beginning,” said Ludwig. “The rest was just silence.”
That was the reason? That I didn't want to become a tram driver? All these years I thought you were disappointed because I left. Because I left Mum on her own.

No. Your mother drove you to Munich, in the Trabant, with all your crates. She was proud of you. And so was I. But I never told you, because I was too proud. I should have told you. On the day you left. I stood at the window and didn't even wave to you.

Thomas said nothing for a long time. Then he got up, went to the apple tree, put his hand on the bark and looked up at the white blossoms. When he turned round, his eyes were wet. “I saw you at the window,” he said quietly. “I waited for you to wave. Mum said: he isn't waving because he's crying. I didn't believe her.”

Ludwig nodded slowly. “She was right. She was always right.” He looked at Leo, who had been sitting the whole time with his head bowed on the garden bench, his hands between his knees, exactly the way Thomas had sat at seventeen. “Thomas,” said Ludwig. “Back then I reproached you for wanting to become something different from me. And now you want to reproach your son for wanting to become the same as me. Do you realise how crazy that is?”

And suddenly Thomas laughed. Quietly at first, then loudly, so loudly that the neighbours in the next garden stopped talking again, this time for different reasons. He laughed until the tears came, and Anja laughed with him, and Paul, and Andrei, and in the end Leo too, who didn't quite know why, but could tell that the storm had passed. Lena came out of the kitchen with the coffee and asked what was so funny. Nobody could explain it to her.

Leo got up and went over to his father. He was a head taller than Thomas, but at that moment he looked like a little boy. “Dad,” he said. “I didn't say no to university because I'm against you. I said it because every time I sat at the front of the tram in Munich I was happy. Just happy. I don't know why. I never felt anything like that when I was studying maths.” Thomas put his hand on his son's shoulder. “You don't have to explain,” he said quietly. “I should have understood that without you explaining. Your grandfather made exactly the same face when he showed me line 46 when I was a child.”
Leo. I shouldn't have reacted like that. It's your life. If you want to drive trams, drive trams. But promise me one thing: be a good tram driver. One who waits until the last person has got on.

Leo looked at his father, then at his grandfather. “That's what Mr Wolff said too,” he said. “At the interview. He said he learnt it from a certain Ludwig Brandt.” Ludwig raised his eyebrows. “Kurt invited you to the interview? Personally?” Leo nodded and blushed. “He said he really wanted to meet the grandson. And then he questioned me for two hours about braking distances and stops. I think I got everything wrong.” Ludwig laughed. “If Kurt questions you for two hours, you've already got the job. He only questions the ones he wants to keep.”

Leo gave a broad smile for the first time that day. And Ludwig, who was leaning on his stick to get up, took something small and shiny out of the inside pocket of his jacket and put it in his grandson's hand. It was an old brass badge, with a little tram on it and the letters “BVB”. “I got it on my first day at work, in 1968,” he said. “From Mr Pohl. I wore it for forty-one years. Now it's yours. But don't pin it on until September. Before that it brings bad luck.”
Somewhere nearby someone started playing the piano, badly, but with great dedication. Ludwig smiled. “Like Mirko back in the day,” he said.

In the evening, when all the others had gone, Thomas and Ludwig sat alone under the apple tree for a while, on two moving boxes, with two bottles of beer that Paul had found in one of the hundred and seventy crates. It was getting dark and cool. The blossoms glowed white in the dusk. “Dad,” said Thomas after a long pause. “I should have come back sooner. Much sooner. We could have had so many Fridays.” Ludwig clinked his bottle against Thomas's. “We have them now,” he said. “And Leo will have them too. With his father. That's more than we had.”
